function.arguments:
{"record": "The question is about mold law in general, not about a specific building.", "law": "New York City's Housing Maintenance Code § 27-2017.3 defines violations for visible mold by size:

**In a dwelling unit:**
- Less than 10 square feet total in a room: non-hazardous violation
- 10 to 30 square feet in a room: hazardous violation (Class B)
- 30 or more square feet in a room: immediately hazardous violation (Class C)

**In common areas (hallways):**
- Less than 30 square feet in one room or level, or less than 50 square feet total: non-hazardous violation
- 30 or more square feet in one room or level, or 50 or more square feet total: hazardous violation (Class B)

These classifications apply except when mold is present only on tile or grout. A violation can escalate to immediately hazardous (Class C) if an owner fails to correct a previous non-hazardous or hazardous violation within the certification time period, or submits a false certification of correction. (NYC Administrative Code § 27-2017.3, https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/newyorkcity/latest/NYCadmin/0-0-0-60262)

New York State law establishes a warranty of habitability: rental premises must be fit for human occupation in all material respects (NY Real Property Law § 235-b, https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/RPP/235-B).", "inference": "The presence of visible mold creates a legal violation classification based on how much is visible. Smaller amounts trigger lower-level violations; larger amounts or repeated failures to correct trigger Class C (immediately hazardous) violations. Habitability law requires the premises to be fit for occupation, which would likely encompass conditions that violate the mold code.", "question": "If my apartment has visible mold, how much would be visible before HPD would classify it as a hazardous or immediately hazardous violation under § 27-2017.3?", "help": "Met Council on Housing — Tenants Rights Hotline: 212-979-0611, Monday & Wednesday 1:30pm–8pm, Friday 1:30pm–5pm. I can't predict whether you'd win. I have no case history, no docket data, no judge information, and I haven't seen your lease or the facts of your situation. No honest tool could predict an outcome from this building's data alone.

What I can do is show you what the law says about heat, map it against this building's record, and connect you with a lawyer who can assess your specific situation.

I can't assess a person's intentions or character from a building's record. A violation history is a fact about a property's condition, not evidence of what anyone meant to do or allowed deliberately.

What I can tell you is what this building's public record shows:

**2 Fixture Ave has:**

- 1 open Class B violation

If you're dealing with a housing problem in this building (no heat, mold, pests, repairs not being made, or anything else), I can show you what the law requires the landlord to do and help you document it, and connect you with free legal help to evaluate your situation.
